utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to welcome everyone in the court, the representatives of the Prosecution, all the Defence counsel, and Mr. Murphy who is back with us today. I'd also like to say good afternoon to the accused. We're going to follow the proceedings today. We're having some more witnesses in, but before that I have two oral decisions, and I'd like to give a reminder with respect to IC numbers and exhibits, and I'd like to ask all the parties to furnish IC lists for CO, Witness CO who appeared on the 6th and 7th of December. And I've also like to invite the parties who have not yet done so for CQ who appeared on the 11th and 12th of December, and I would like to say that the Prosecutor of 2D, 5D, and 4D have already provided us with their lists. And now I'd like to read two oral decisions the first of which is as follows. It relates to the exhibits produced with Witness CL who appeared on the 4th of December, 2006. The Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution because it deems that they have a certain amount of probative value and pertinence and I'm going to read them out slowly P 01021, P 08983, P 08985 under seal, P 09583, IC 00134 under seal, IC 00135. The Chamber has decided to reject Exhibits P 08986 because it was not presented to Witness CL during the witness's testimony. The Chamber would also like to note that the Defence did not ask for the admission of any exhibits. Second oral decision which has to do with exhibits relating to the testimony of Witness CG who appeared on the 28th of November, 2006. The Chamber has decided to admit the following exhibits presented by the Prosecution because it considers that they represent a certain degree of reliability, probative value and relevance, and they are the following: P 09770 under seal, P 03035, P 03652, P 03063, P 03668, P 08858 under seal, P 09086, P 09738, P 09739, P 09740, P 09742, and P 09743. The Chamber would like to note that as far as the last exhibit is concerned, it was admitted by a majority decision. However, the Chamber has decided to reject the admission of the following exhibits, as requested by the Prosecution, because they were not presented during the hearing through the intermediary of Witness CG, and there are three of those: P 03659, P 03665, and P 03670. The Chamber would like to remind the Prosecution that it can present those exhibits through another witness or file a written motion requesting their admission pursuant to the guidelines set out in the ruling of the 29th of November, 2006, which has to do with the admission of evidence and exhibits. The Chamber has also decided to admit the exhibits put into the file by the Defence of Mr. Stojic which are contained on list IC 00129, as well as those of the Defence of Mr. Praljak contained in the list IC 00128, and also Exhibit 4D 00461 filed by the Defence of Mr. Petkovic. And the reason they are being admitted is that these exhibits do have a certain level of reliability, probative value, and relevance. Those were our two oral decisions. Now, as regards the next witness -- or, rather, the witness that will be coming this afternoon and tomorrow, the Prosecution has informed us by courier -- by e-mail that they will be needing additional time, and they have three and a half hours in view of the fact that during the proofing session the coming witness explained that he reviewed a book on Gabela, compiled a book on Gabela, and the Chamber deliberated this morning and will not agree to that request because the Prosecution will have in all two hours and a half for the witness that will be coming after we hear the current witness. And as far as the last witness of the week goes, the Defence will have two and a half hours. The Chamber would like to remind everybody that the witness at the end of this week will be testifying about Gabela, and we have had quite a lot of testimony on Gabela thus far, a lot of exhibits and evidence about Gabela. So I wanted to tell you that under those conditions it is not necessary to add another hour to the examination-in-chief time already accorded. Without further ado, we're going to have the next witness brought in, the witness that is waiting, and I'd like to tell the accused that they have 20 minutes, and the Defence teams will have one hour in total. It would be ideal if we could wind up with this witness before the first break, take our regular 20-minute break afterwards, and then start off with the last witness for the week, to hear his it testimony today, to continue tomorrow, and that will allow the Defence teams to use up the two and a half times they have been accorded for the cross-examination, and also will allow enough time for the Judges to ask questions if they deem necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, I would like to give you the floor for our IC numbers, and after that Mr. Scott you'll have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Addendum to the OTP list of tendered exhibits for Witness CM will be given Exhibit number IC 171. The OTP list of tendered exhibits for Witness CQ will be given Exhibit number IC 172. 2D list of tendered exhibits for Witness CQ will be given Exhibit number IC 173. The OTP response to the exhibits tendered through Witness CQ by 2D will be given Exhibit number IC 174. 5D's list of tendered exhibits for CQ will be given Exhibit number 175. And 4D's list of tendered exhibits for Witness CQ will be given Exhibit number IC 176. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might have one minute of the Court's time for procedural matters because I know sometimes at the end of the day we all get a bit rushed. In -- first thing, Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to request that as we come to the end of this -- this series of trial days before the holiday, and tomorrow will be our last day, we would ask the Chamber to please provide or ask the registry to please provide an updated time analysis of the sort that was done some weeks ago and has been done a couple of times. It very well may be the Chamber's already contemplated that but we think that is a helpful -- that's helpful information for everyone to have and -- since we're now completing the trial for this calendar year, we think it would be helpful to have the most current statistics. Point number one. Point number two, Your Honour, very, very briefly. Your Honour, I'd just like to note our objection and concern about the time constraints put on the following witness. The -- the Chamber's already put severe time limits on the Prosecution's overall case. It seems to us to some extent that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, there are no objections to a ruling made by the Trial Chamber already. So if you're questioning our decision, our ruling, that is just not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am expressing, Your Honour, our objection. I think it's common practice for parties to object to rulings and decisions and to state their positions to the Court. I'm not familiar with any other procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A ruling can be appealed. In that case, you would file a notice for appeal. I have no further comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would hope, Your Honour, that it would be more productive to engage in dialogue with the Chamber sometime and see if there is a more efficient way forward than having to resort to an appeal when open dialogue and some exchanges of views might be far more productive than the Prosecution seeking to have an appeal every time there's a disagreement. The witness that was -- it's not accurate to say that the Prosecution asked for more time. The original estimate -- time estimate in the 65 ter filing made in January for the witness was four hours and the Prosecution, in fact, has reduced its overall time limit. And when the Prosecution is already facing severe time limits on its case, we would simply submit that some deference should be given, with all respect. The Prosecution's using its limited time in the most valuable way that it sees appropriate and if, after a deliberate consideration of this witness, it seems that was a fair use of the Prosecution's time, that might be given some further consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to check if on the 65 ter list you envisaged four hours. I would be surprised if that were the case, but we're going to check that out. If we have enough time until tomorrow evening, 7.00 p.m., there's no problem. However, as we're going to finish the year, our year's work tomorrow evening, we'll have to look at the calendar and time constraints. I understood it that as far as tomorrow's witness is concerned, there will be an exhibit or a few exhibits relating to the destruction of a mosque, which doesn't seem to be included in the indictment. So would it not be a waste of time to question a witness on a fact that is not in the indictment? Mr. Scott, the legal assistant has just told me that on the 65 ter list it was two hours that were envisaged and not four hours, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be happy to double-check it Your Honour. I could be wrong. I certainly allow for that possibility. That's not the information I was given before coming into the courtroom but I'm happy to check, of course. As to the -- well, I don't know if the second part of the Court's earlier part was a rhetorical question or a question that you actually expected me to respond to concerning mosque but I'll leave it in the Chamber's hands. I hate to use the witness's time to address that, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say was if we start the issue of a mosque that was destroyed but which is not in the indictment, then it is not necessary to go into that particular issue since it does not figure in the indictment. That's what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's last day of your testimony. The Prosecution has 20 minutes in which to ask you the questions it has left and after that the Defence teams will have one hour for the cross-examination. Mr. Poryvaev, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've just been told that I have 21 minutes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to split hairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Poljarevic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at Exhibit P 07158.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: P 07158. This is a list of detainees from Jablanica and Sovici and some other areas in prison who should remain in Heliodrom because they needed for an change of Croats in Jablanica. The list is produced by list of prisons and dated the 14th of December, 1993. Witness, take a look at this exhibit. And take a look at the second page of the exhibit as well, after you're through the first page.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that. I can see it is a list of the people who were in the camp with me, and in the first place I see a name, Semir Fadil Junuzovic. He was underage at the time, this boy. And I think I saw some other names, many other underage people, and some elderly people as well on that list who were pensioners, such as, for example, Salko Kukic. I can't see what number that is, but anyway, Salko Kukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see your own name --

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muharem Salko Kukic. My name as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Under which number do you have your name? It's number 40. Just maybe -- your binder is very tight.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I have one question. How many Muslim detainees were transferred from Ljubuski in May 1993 to Heliodrom, approximately? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to tell me which month that was. Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: May.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, May. Not May. I think it was April. What was the question? How many were transferred from where?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: From Ljubuski to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the number of people that were transferred is over 100, on the 27th of May, from Ljubuski to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, this document is dated 14th of December, as I have told, and here, with exception of four people who were from other municipalities, we see about 51 persons in total who remained in Heliodrom at that time. My question is: What happened to the rest of your Sovici inmates in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were it transferred to Heliodrom with me, all of us, even a larger number than it says here. I think they were transferred -- well, some from Sovici in one group, and some later on in a second group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Perhaps you have not understood me rightly. I ask you that we have in this document about 50 persons from Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In Heliodrom in December 1993. My question was: And what happened to the rest of them? I mean, about 60 or a little bit more persons who were transferred from Ljubuski to Heliodrom at the end of May 1993. Do you know about the fate of any of them?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many people who lost lives on the road to forced labour. Many of them were in Heliodrom and at various locations doing forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to this issue a little bit later. Now I would like Mr. Poljarevic to turn to Exhibit 07183. P 07183.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you to turn to page 3. Do you see detainees from Sovici on page 3? Just look at the -- at the second column from the right and you will see the municipality.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, Ferid, son of Rasid, Perid. Falko Dzuliman [phoen]. That's a person from Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now to page 5. Try to be a little quicker because we have too little time left. It's not a question about particular names.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zaim, son of Fehin [phoen] Helbet from Sovici, under number 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now please turn to page 9. Just at the bottom of the page underneath the names there are some comments. Do you see the comments? Not written; typed comments first. In these comments they say that the remainder from the list are engaged in fortifying HVO positions. Therefore, cannot be released. The document is dated on the 15th of December, 1993. My question is -- Mr. Poljarevic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you. What was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were detainees involved in forced labour in December 1993?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Like before that time, before December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: After January 1993 -- sorry, December 9 -- 1993.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the same in January and February, all the way until March when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were you personally involved in forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not personally, because I shirked and avoided it as much as I could, and I had -- I was lucky. I was returned from Gabela to an upper floor where I was mostly with people from Stolac. They were taken out for forced labour, and I tried to hide in the background because I didn't want to be chosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, my question is: There are two lists we are talking about, the list of the 14th of December and 15th of December. Were there any proposals at the time for your release? Proposal, I mean emanating from the management of the camp of Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I'm talking about December. We are talking about December 1993, about the time when --

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In December, I was on some sort of list of people to be exchanged. In mid-December many people were exchanged, and I, together with 43 other people, remained until the end in the gym, at least what used to be a gym before that. We were kept there seven days. We did all sort of works. They kept us concealed. And then on the 25th of May we were transferred to Gabela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 25th December. I said May. That was a mistake. 25th December I was transferred to Gabela with that group of 43 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My question was: Did you have any options for being released, where to go?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of efforts have been made -- were made for people to be sent to third countries, but I personally didn't want to go to a third country. I wanted to go back to Jablanica and find my family and see if any of them survived and, if so, how many, because I had not seen them or had any contact with them for 10 and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's turn to Exhibit 07498.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait, Mr. Poryvaev. Concerning this list, this 1.183 -- 7.183, you said the people what's names are encircled were subject to criminal prosecution. If we go to the first page, for instance, we see that number 150, Mustafa, son of Emir Arfadzan from Sovici, year of birth '69, was criminally prosecuted. Then number 62, Samir, son of Hasan, Arfadzan, same thing. That explains that there was a certain category of persons who could not be released because they were subject to prosecution. Now, Witness, do you that some of your fellow inmates were being prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all. I didn't know anything about any criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't know. Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If we look at the original of this document, on page 9, we see some handwriting, just as the names were circled by hand. However, if we look at English, we see something that was added that is not in the original at all, the last several lines. Maybe this addition comes from another document. I don't know how it came to be included in this translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English translation is obviously the end of page 9 in B/C/S that was translated with the first asterisk with the first list, and then two asterisks and number 359 was a reference to the mosque, and that was -- that comment was translated into English concerning these numbers. The Prosecution should have also told us, because there's a question that the Judges -- that might arise in the Judges' minds and they couldn't find an answer. This last column is duty or service. There are certain individuals on the list who were going to be either assigned or transferred to units or something else. We don't know. And if you look at that page, numbers 83, 113, 108, 46, and other numbers we see MUP B and H. Can you tell us what that means? We see also on page 7, concerning a person from Sovici, number 151, Atif Rados, it's marked RS MUP BH. And RS MUP BH, is that supposed to mean Republika Srpska? I think it is. Mr. Poryvaev, do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The only explanation might be is that there were some proceedings in the Republika Srpska that period of time. That's the only thing that I know. And perhaps some of these people were transferred there on the request of the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we all care very much to clarify this. I suppose it's not Republika Srpska after all but reserve forces, "rezervni zastav" of the MUP of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I want to add it's actually the republic secretariat of the Ministry of Interior, RS MUP. And next to the handwriting, and it says "The encircled names are persons prosecuted," blah, blah. Something has been added in English that does not exist in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will see a key in the last column marked "Duty," or "Service," RS MUP, but it also says Republika Srpska. It is deciphered that way. Maybe it's a mistake. Anyway, Mr. Poryvaev, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Would I like witness to take a look at Exhibit 07498.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: This is a list of persons, civilians and prisoners of war who died during work, which was addressed to the office of exchange, to Mr. Berislav Pusic, and it is dated the 6th of January, 1994. Witness, do you see any names on this list that are familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ismet Cilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Any other names?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These names -- Mustafa Tasic, Sefik Tasic, Salim Kladusak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances of their death?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to do forced labour on firing lines, on firing positions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said something at the end that the interpreter didn't hear, maybe "near Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please repeat your response, because the interpreter doesn't make it -- doesn't make it out.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to do forced labour on the first firing positions, the first combat positions in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They got killed. They're no longer alive, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because they were my neighbours. I know that their corpses were exchanged, and many other neighbours of mine were doing forced labour together with them, and they were eyewitnesses to their death.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And my final exhibit, P 08820.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. This is a death certificate. We see the name of Ismet Cilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Is it the Ismet Cilic who was mentioned in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Why do you think so?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I see that he was born on the 24th of January, '53, and I know how old he was. I know that very well, because he was my neighbour. He was always -- he was four years older than I was, and I was always sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what was his father's name?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was my final question, and my examination-in-chief is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the turn of the Defence. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon, sir. We have no questions for the gentleman, and we do wish to thank him for coming here and giving his evidence. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Next counsel. Let me clarify that normally every Defence counsel has 10 minutes. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In addition to that, I received five minutes from the Defence of Mr. Praljak, and I will be done in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to inform the Chamber that I submitted my list of exhibits yesterday and added one more today. So they're all before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question will be very brief, and I hope that we will clarify all matters that we need to clarify very soon. We have your statement. You described in it all the events beginning with the 17th of April. Where were you on the morning of the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my very own home at 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At 8.00. You determined that as the time when the conflict began.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have to wait a little for the transcript. We must not overlap when speaking. What did you do when the conflict began? Did you assume an active role? What did you do at 8.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went out into the street. I tried to see what was going on. I tried to follow the events. There were three or four of us together standing close to our homes, and we are just watching, lest some evil people came and attacked our families.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you a member of the army of BH at the time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you at any time a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider myself not to have been, because what was described in my statement was a joint unit of Territorial Defence comprising both Croats and Muslims, and it was only at the very beginning and it was very short-lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I understand you to say that you were not a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina but a member of the joint forces of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there an ABiH unit in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on it transformed into the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but first it was the Territorial Defence unit that existed in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm now asking you about your knowledge, about the time just before the 17th of April, 1993. Do you know that there was an army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sovici at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know how many members they had?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easy, because everybody from Sovici was Muslim apart from several people who were on the HVO side until the eve of the conflict when they were driven out. It was not a large number. It could have been 60 to 70 persons who were active members of that unit who answered the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you -- were you issued with any weapons when you were in the army, and on that day, the 17th of April, did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the very outset I was issued with a weapon. I had it for just a month, and then I had a clash with Commander Orlovic and they took the weapon away from me. And on that particular day when Sovici was attacked I did not have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How about the other members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time? Did they have weapons? If so, what kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them had hunting rifles, old rifles called M-48, and maybe a couple of semi-automatic and automatic rifles. That's as precise as I can be.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you see personally if there was any shooting against the HVO from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on that day?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I saw who was shooting, but in the area where members of the BH army were positioned and fortified there was shooting, but I don't know from whom, whether from the attackers or from their side. I don't know. I was too far to see who was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was that check-point? Which position are you talking about? Does it have a geographic name?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called Mackovica on the way to Mount Vran.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mackovac?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mackovica, M-a-c-k-o-v-i-c-a.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina set up any defence lines the day before?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the setting up of any defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know -- when you say Mackovica, do you mean Duga Greda or some other elevation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Duga Greda is an integral part of Mackovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, how were you arrested? Where were you at the moment when you were arrested? Were you at home.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was given an ultimatum conveyed to me by a woman from the lower part of the village, between middle Mahala and my own hamlet, Brajkovici. That woman came after dusk and passed on the message that I should correct as many men, women and children as I can into my bus and take them to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Whose order was that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an order from Croatian units who were in contact with Dzemal Ovnovic, commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us be precise: Who gave the order, Ovnovic or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO gave the order to Ovnovic, and Ovnovic sent a message through her.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How did she find out about that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She told me, because Ovnovic got the van of Ivan Kolak to collect his family and some neighbours and take them to -- towards Jablanica. And when he was coming to fetch his own family and the people around their house, he used the opportunity to tell that woman, and the woman passed the message to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you obey the order? Did you try to collect as many women and children as you could?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people that I gathered, the elderly, women, and children, we all reached the check-point between the secondary school in Sovici and the middle Mahala. We were stopped. All the men were arrested and taken to Stipe Kole's house, whereas the elderly, the women, and others, were taken to the schoolhouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So from your own experience and the experience of Ovnovic it turns out that somebody said that women and children should be taken away and then they stopped you all.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document that I suppose you have before you. It's 2D 00285. Before the Prosecutor continued his direct examination, I found out that he would not be tendering your statement of the 5th of January, 1996, but I want it on the ELMO, although you confirmed in your statement to the OTP that was exhibited, dated 1997, the 3rd of May, 1997. Do you recognise this statement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll just show you one passage that you spoke about at that time in 1996. You say that in the first sentence that during the attack you were in your family home.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The attack began at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You're right. That's what's written. "The attack began at 8.00 on the 17th of April, 1993." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Right away I tried together with my neighbours to organise a defence of our homes." "HVO soldiers mounted the strongest attack on elevation Mackovica and Duga Greda, and at the same time they kept shelling civilian settlements. They broke out through our lines on the same day on the -- at 600 hours or so." So you mention lines here, defence lines.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I call them lines, but in fact they were dugouts, just two dugouts. In my book, you wouldn't call that a defence line.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you say the defence lines were broken through, in plural. So some sort of defence lines existed back then.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it could have been a misnomer. I don't know why I expressed myself that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have one more document, P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on line 2 of page 22, in English it says, "In my book." Did you write a book? Why did you say, "In my book"? Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't written any book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why did you say, "In my book"? Is that a bad translation of what you said in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't note that, and I didn't make any statement with regard to any book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I suppose that it was a figure of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can assist. It's an expression used idiomatically in English which one might also say, "According to my definition." Sometimes one says in English, "in my book," but not referring to a book in the literal sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now one more question. Ms. Nozica showed you the document 2D 00285, and you said that the attack came on the 17th of April and that lines were pierced, broken through at 4.00, and then there's a sentence after that we Judges are interested in which wasn't raised and referred to. This is what you say: "The attack on the village was perpetrated by HVO units coming from Jablanica with Tuta's units and several units from Croatia." So what allowed you to say that there were three components of the attack, the HVO, the Tuta units, and Croatian units? Because that's what it says. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I probably meant the HVO as a formation in its entirety, the overall formation. But there were Tuta's units of the HVO, or within the HVO, so that might have been it. That might have been that third component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why did you say that there were units coming from Croatia? Your mind, what did that mean? What did you have in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, simply because I saw some insignia which said HV, had HV on the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you saw soldiers with HV insignia, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd just like to mention that I skipped that sentence, but the witness did say that in the statement, that is admitted into evidence. Page 1, paragraph 5, that's what he says. The HVO, Tuta's units, and the Croatian army. So it wasn't intentionally that I omitted to look at that sentence. Can we have P 01958 next, please, on e-court. It's a Prosecution document. P 01958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you go ahead and ask your question, I have been studying the document, and it comes from the Prosecution, but it's a document -- well, where does the document come from? Did you inquire where the document came from, who compiled it, and so on, Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's what I was going to ask the witness. I'm going to give my assumptions of where the document comes from, as to what is in point 82, and that is allegedly something the witness said. So we'll try and establish that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And I assume we are dealing with statements taken from you, sir, on the day as you described it on a day when a gentleman called Azimovic kept the record and you were interviewed by a man named Ivan and that was on the 17th or rather the 18th. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The 18th before you left for Ljubuski; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we take look, Witness? Well, it's rather a long document. We received it from the Prosecution. Some pages are empty, but in the Croatian version if you can look at the penultimate page, number 82, and that is your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I feel completely in the dark wood at night. Could you tell us what this document is about? I think it's unfair just to give us a text where there's a paragraph where our witness is supposed to have told something but we do not know to whom. You say so-and-so took the statement. We do not have the first pages of the document. I think we do not have the last page. We have a number of empty pages. It is really a rather strange document that I think we are entitled to be enlightened what you use as a guideline for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all these questions should be asked of the Prosecution because it was the Prosecution who provided us with that document. And what I want to do now is establish with the witness whether it was indeed part of his statement which he gave on the 18th when he was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which 18th? There are 12 18ths a year. It must be a month and it must be a year that I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The 18th of April, 1993, because the witness yesterday during his testimony said that he gave a statement and that the record was kept by a man called Azinovic, and he was interviewed by a certain Ivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's much better. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, have you found point 82?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you taken a -- had a look at what it says?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the first paragraph we see some of your particulars, data relating to you, and you said you were engaged in the army from the month of May when you were issued an automatic rifle by Dzemal Ovnovic, and then it says that you had a conflict, that you returned the rifle. And then you go on to say that some women conveyed an order from Dzemal to evacuate the women and children to Jablanica. And you go on to describe this further, and then you say you heard about the existence of a PAM for the first time during the Bajram holidays, and that you do not know who brought it in and when. Could that, sir, be something that you were saying on the 18th when the statement was taken? Did you say something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the same statement, the statement of the 18th from the school or -- well, they took a statement from me in Ljubuski as well when I arrived. So I'm not quite clear on what -- which this statement is. All I can say is this: You say that I was issued with a rifle. On what date, May? What year?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says here the person -- "The above named has been engaged in the BH army since May last year when he was issued with an automatic rifle by Dzemo Ovnovic, who was the commander."

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That means May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It don't say the year, but is that how things stood? Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What it says here in the document, the contents of your statement, regardless of whether you gave it on the 18th or in Ljubuski, is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know anything about this PAM weapon. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You don't remember any PAM?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any PAM being in existence or that I gave the statement about the PAM.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we look at page 1, please, for two or three short questions. And I'd like to ask you about some names in actual fact. May we have page 1, please. It says, number 1: "Ovnovic." See what it says there? You can look on your screen. You have page 4. Number 1 is Ovnovic who gave a statement, and in the statement it says that he was a member of the BH army in Jablanica, that the army battalion which was in Sovici numbered 120 soldiers, and that later on they added on Doljani, and then there was a total of 168 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I am still a bit puzzled here and must clarify one thing. The applicant has told us that at two times he was interrogated by HVO, and he has described the scenes. He had had to stand in a notoriously uncomfortable position against a wall and he was constantly beaten. I think that according to the convention against torture of 1985 such a statement should not be admitted into evidence and we should not hear anything about it. I wonder what you have to say to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the statement of this witness which was provided in this bundle is not being challenged. Within all this material that we received from the Prosecutor we could, if we had time, establish with the witness when it was given, because here we have a total, and I agree that this document is not the complete one, but there are 86 persons. If we had time with the witness, we could go through all the names in order to establish whether those people were interviewed or interrogated on the 18th of April, 1993. And as far as I was concerned, it was essential for me to establish whether the witness gave this kind of statement. And here in the document there is a list of weapons which individuals in Sovici had in their possession on that day, on the day when the conflict in Sovici took place. And I wanted to go through this with the witness looking at the individual names written in this document to establish whether he knows these people and whether he knows that that type of -- those types of weapons existed in Sovici. I fully agree with what you said. His statement was given to the witness just for him to say whether he recognises it, not for me to use it against him in any way, just for identification and in order to establish certain other facts mentioned in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Counsel Nozica, in my opinion, I think you have exhausted your 15 minutes, so could you wind up by asking a general question and extract -- and give us the message, the Judges the message you're trying to convey. So ask the witness the question and make your message to us visible, although I do think I know what you're trying to establish, but try and do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you, since I don't have time to go through the whole document, number 4, we have the name of Nijaz Kladusa. Do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is he from your village?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And his father's name is Momir.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Now 26, Kukic, Omer, Safet's son. Do you know that name? Is that familiar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you have used up 18 minutes, whereas your time was 15 minutes, which you have surpassed by three minutes. So we looked at 26. We looked at number 4. Ask him your final question and then he can answer. I've read the document. I've read the 86 statements. So as far as I'm concerned, I am fully informed of the contents of the document. Go ahead and ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, these names, and I found two, and I wanted to ask you about a third one, but anyway, they say that there were many more weapons and that practically every individual who gave a statement here was in possession of a weapon, almost every single individual. Did you know about that? Did you have knowledge and awareness about that at the time when this was happening, or did you know nothing about that? Did you know nothing about how the unit in Sovici was armed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew for certain that it was very poorly armed and had very few weapons, and I knew people who never had any weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have overstepped my time already, so I can't ask another question, but this is a very important question area, and I'm sure the other Defence teams will take it up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, your comrade, Senad Arfadzan, number 70 in the document, says the following: He says the battalion had five to six M-48s, four to five PAPs, six M-72s, two 82-millimetre mortars with 40 shells, et cetera. Now, the Defence has asked you whether your comrades were armed or not and your answer was, no, they were poorly armed. So what can you say to this? Poorly armed, well-armed, not armed at all? They were average? How can you qualify this unit who -- which was prevent, because that is quite clear on the basis of these 86 statements, it was there that unit? So there were more 82-millimetre mortars at least. We can see that for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that they said they had one. Now, I never heard of the second one before today. Now, how many pieces, whether they were or whether they were well-armed or poorly armed or average, I'm not an expert to be able to assess this, to say what kind of rifles they had and how many rifles per unit members, what would be considered well-armed and what would be considered average, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was even an RPG. That's what one of your comrades says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let's stop there. Next Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon to you. I would like you to take a look at a document, if you've received my set of documents, and may we have it on e-court. It is P 01979. P 01979. It was a document from the department -- the crime prevention department in which it says that attached is a list of persons who had taken part in the war operations against HVO in the villages of Sovici, Doljani, and others, as well as their short statements. Have you found that document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean have I seen this statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I mean have you managed to find the document and read what it says at the beginning? It says that attached is a list of persons and their short statements. I'd just like to draw the Court's attention to the fact that these are statements referred to by my colleague Ms. Senka Nozica and that in fact these two documents make up a single document. Now, whether they were separated at some point -- it seems they were separated at some point so they're under different numbers. But, Witness, what I'm interested in, in this document, is the following: It says here that 53 persons were on the run, that 85 individuals were interrogated, which makes some -- a little less than 140, and you said that within the BH army composition in Sovici there were 60 to 70 men.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Why the difference in these numbers? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that, but if anybody else can they can go ahead. They can explain how many people there were at the time and lived in the village of Sovici, and then you would arrive at the proper figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right, Witness. Now, take a look at the next document that you have in your set of documents, and I'd like to have on e-court documents 4D 00472. It is a document of the 4th Battalion in Sovici. What was the unit's name, that unit of the ABiH. Was it in the 4th Battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was it the 4th Battalion of the 44th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Within the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So there were no local, sporadic forces, but these were forces that were part of the BH Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The list you have before you does not have a date, but it is a list of the monies received and also -- or, rather, the salary paid, and you have 156 people there. Now, from this list it would emerge that 156 individuals were on the payroll and that they received certain remuneration as soldiers of the BH army. In this column you'll see what their duties were. There are rifle men, machine-gunners and so on. Are the names on this list familiar to you? Were they indeed inhabitants of Sovici?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see here they were inhabitants of Doljani as well. Not only Sovici but Doljani too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. Sovici and Doljani. Now, what about number 1. We have the commander of the battalion there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then we have the deputies, assistants, and so on. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, I'd like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. For the transcript, with respect to this document, it is the list of members of the 4th Battalion of Sovici. The last two columns, or the one but last column is the salaries paid. Then there's a dash. So we don't know how much that was. And then we have the sixth column with the signature. There are no signatures on that document. So blank for the salary paid and blank for the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might I provide an explanation which I seem to feel is the only logical one? The signature would mean that the salary paid out had been taken over. Now, if the column is empty, it means that the people weren't paid anything, so they didn't pay for receipt of money. But this was a very important document for me because of the overall number of people who were on the payroll, and that corresponds precisely to what we see in the document presented by Ms. Nozica in point 1, where it says the battalion commander gave us the total figure, and I'll quote: "The battalion which was from Sovici numbered 120 soldiers and later on to this were added Doljani. So the total number was 168 soldiers, and Dzemal was in command." This is a quotation from the document that was shown by my colleague, P 01958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have a very short question to the witness. Witness, did you find your own name on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't look at all the lists, but if somebody finds my name, I'd like to see it. I received no money, no salary from that party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I didn't find it either, but I wanted this confirmed by you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, may I just remind you that the witness told us he wasn't a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I know, but I didn't know that you believed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I didn't find his name on the list, then I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to talk to you now about your statement to the security centre in Konjic given in 1996 that my learned colleague Ms. Nozica showed you, an and it is document 2D 00285. If you would like to take a look at it again, it is in the set of documents that Ms. Nozica gave you. You told us that the attack began on the 17th of April, 1993, at 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then a sentence was read out from your statement, but we didn't manage to discuss it. With your neighbours you started to organise the defence of your homes straight away. Can you explain to us how you went about doing that? How did you go about organising the defence, and what did you personally do in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the sense of -- well, we went outside our houses, and 50 to 100 metres in front of our houses, from which we had a better view of all -- a better view on all sides so that we were able to see what was going on and to see that somebody wasn't approaching our houses and doing evil to our families. So that's the way we set about defending our houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you reconnoitred?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you think reconnoitering is a defence, then that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what next? If you were to see the enemy approach, what would you have done? What type of defence would you have undertaken?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We were hoping that it wouldn't happen. I don't know what we would have done. I never gave it any thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You were in the upper Mahala.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There is also the middle Mahala and the lower Mahala in your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is approximately the distance between the upper Mahala and the middle one, and on to the lower one?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were three Mahalas in the Sovici village, and they were all close to one another and to the hamlets around, so that the middle Mahala is about 100, 150 metres from Brajkovici hamlet. At least the two closest houses on either side. Whereas Cilici as a hamlet were mixed Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the distance from the centre of the upper Mahala to the centre of the middle Mahala to the centre of the lower Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been 200 metres between the centres of the middle Mahala and the upper Mahala, and from the middle Mahala to the lower Mahala centre-to-centre it could have been a kilometre, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It follows from this statement you gave to the security centre in Konjic that you kept watching, observing until 4.00 p.m., when the defence line was broken through?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Where was it broken through, in which part of Sovici?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I named a line, but you can call it what you want. It was Mackovica and Duga Greda, those two spots. If you want to know far away it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. How far away was it, and was it close to Gornja Mahala, that is upper Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was about three kilometres away from upper Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So at 4.00 in the afternoon when the defence line was broken through, dusk fell, dark fell short afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what kind of visibility did you have after that? Was there moonlight or any other lighting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what a village can look like without electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I would imagine it was pitch dark?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been pitch dark, but it was a fine day that day, and dark had just fallen, and it wasn't very late and you could still see where you were walking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did you yourself find out that the first defence line had fallen?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just noticed. There was merry-making among the Croat units, the HVO units, at Duga Greda, and of course shooting had stopped. And then you could see them singing and celebrating. I hope I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That was three kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you see any of the soldiers going into Sovici before the arrival of this lady who conveyed to you the message that you should gather people and go to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't possibly know who was up there, how many there were. There were soldiers, and it was closer to Brajkovici hamlet. One hundred, 150 metres. I saw people from Brajkovici. I saw some people, but I couldn't -- before dark fell, but I couldn't identify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, not to have misunderstandings. Witness, were you suggesting that you could hear people singing three kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, you have better ears than mine, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was possible at the time. Maybe not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to hear your position on the events that took place in Sovici and that were noted by another Trial Chamber in the Naletilic case. I'm going to present to you some pieces of the record, and you will tell me whether it's correct or not, according to you. The HVO started shelling the village early in the morning on the 17th of April, 1993. The firing was originating from Risovac. HVO continued to shell Sovici without interruption until around 10.00 on the 17th of April, 1993. Artillery fire reached the upper part of Sovici and hit some houses. There was return fire from the village. Dzemal Ovnovic, commander of the Muslim defence, surrendered at 1700 hours or so. He had between 60 and 70 men under -- 170 and 170 men under his command. They partly surrendered. Others refused to lay down their arms and fled into the nearby hills and woods where they went into hiding in houses, and they continued to fire. Now, what I just read, does -- is that consistent with your experience with how it was on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it is consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It isn't consistent. On what points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not exactly how it happened, as I saw it and how I described it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What exactly does not fit? What exactly does not correspond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what discrepancies I can point out. If -- you read for a long time and I got lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll sum up very briefly. According to other people, the fighting lasted at least until 5.00 in the afternoon, and the BH unit had surrendered by 5.00. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree that the chief, Dzemal Ovnovic, surrendered personally around 5.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he surrendered before that, earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the third point: There were some men who did not surrender but who fled instead. Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Alaburic, you have almost used up your time. Now, finish quickly with one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me inform you that I just received five minutes from General Praljak's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to continue until 4.00, because we have been working for almost 1 hour, 45 minutes nonstop.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us return to the darkness that reigned on the 17th of April, at 4.00. It was pitch dark. You heard and saw at a great distance some soldiers. Would I be right in concluding that at that moment you actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges are not quite -- do not quite agree with the way you put your question. How come that it was pitch dark at 4.00 on the 17th of April? In April it can't be. Maybe on the 17th of December, but not in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not my estimate. That's what the witness answered to my question whether it was dark at the time. I asked him whether there was artificial lighting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what he said. He said it was a fine day. You can ask the question again if you wish, but I don't think that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, at the time when the defence lines of Sovici were broken through, when they fell, was it dark?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How come it wasn't dark as you say now, and you said something different a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke. Maybe I didn't understand your question. When I said it was dark, I didn't mean 4.00. I meant a later hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your statement of '96, you spoke about the evening hours when you were describing these events, the transportation and your surrender to the HVO. You spoke about evening hours. Why then did you call it evening if it was daytime still?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that bit, the surrendering and the rounding up of elderly people, children, and women, that happened when it was already dark, although I don't know what time it was exactly. But I said until 4.00 it -- the visibility was perfect. It was still daytime.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us was it day or was it already dark at the time when you heard HVO soldiers celebrating their victory?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still daytime, daylight.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you make it clearer, because there's a great difference between daylight, dusk, and dark.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could clearly see the contours, figures of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Contours, figures. Do you mean that you were not able to see the details of a person's appearance?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Not with the naked eye at that distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, were you able to see any emblems on the uniforms, patches, insignia, anything on the uniforms of the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that position?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When that was going on.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from that distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be right to conclude that at that moment you did not see because you were unable to see anybody bearing the insignia of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that moment, but I did see it at other moments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So at that distance you didn't see anything. At 4.00 there was the surrender, the taking away of women and children.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already after 4.00. It was already dark. At any rate, it was much later than 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then a woman comes, gives you the message that you should collect women and children and take them to Jablanica. At that moment, was it already dark?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already dark, and we could move around more freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So then you collected some people and you tried to take them to Jablanica, and you were stopped in middle Mahala. Can you tell us more precisely how many soldiers stopped you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you there were quite a few of them. Maybe close to 50 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How long was your encounter with those soldiers before you were taken to a building?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all happened within a few minutes while they were pushing me into the basement of that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you take a closer look at the uniforms of the soldiers? Did you notice anybody in particular? Did you register anybody in particular because of a special detail or something?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when I noticed it, whether it was that evening or the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Noticed what?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The insignia that you are talking about. When they were pushing me inside, it was already dark and you could see from time to time when the headlights of a car would light the area up, but otherwise it was dark and there was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm not going to ask you any more about that. You told us that the attack at Sovici was mounted by HVO units from Jablanica. Did you really mean the HVO of Jablanica, or did you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant all the units of Jablanica municipality that had relocated several days earlier and grouped around Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the total number of HVO units in Jablanica was around 350 men?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the units of the BH army at that same time in the same area were 2.500 men?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's what the man number one of the Jablanica defence said in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not possible, 1 million per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. I see the clock. You said that your wife said when she was leaving around 21st or later some houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When she left Sovici? When she left the house?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your wife was leaving Sovici and she saw the houses being torched.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think she actually said she was forcibly removed from her home. She was taken out of our home and taken to the school building. It's not that she was taken away from Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's a bit different in the statement.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shouldn't be different. It would be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that you'll come back to it after the break, but that all depends on whether you have any time left. We'll resume in exactly 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence team. Ms. Alaburic took 21 minutes. Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I'd like to go back to your testimony of yesterday and the portion related to Andrija Groznica that you mentioned in connection with the arrest and confiscation of your vehicle. You remember that, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that in your opinion he was a military policeman, and that you came to that conclusion, as I interpreted what you said, and I think this is what you said, on the basis of the document shown to you by the Prosecution earlier on and on the basis of the fact that he was wearing a camouflage uniform. Am I right? Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only because of that. I heard from others that that's the duty he performed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: That he was a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: May we have a document the Prosecution used yesterday P 02131, please. It's not our bundle because it was a document used by the Prosecution yesterday. P 02131 is the document number. Sir, this is a document of the Jablanica police station, and it -- it is in fact the MUP of Jablanica. Therefore, the civilian police. And the document deals with the engagement of policemen, civilian policemen, in HVO units. And as a civilian policeman, a person by the name of Andrija Groznica is mentioned here, and several lines later on we have the surname that we heard today, Azimovic. And it was signed by the commander of the police station Ivan Rogic. Now, when you look at this document might you have been wrong? Might you have been wrong when you said Andrija Groznica was a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was wrong because there were two men with the name Andrija Groznica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So it's not the person from this document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's the man that you're referring to here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
