utterances.text: Right. Not the man. Now, I'd like to go and discuss the events that took place at the mechanical engineering faculty. Yesterday, you said in your statement, and I'd like to go back to when you were talking about the mistreatment of you at the faculty and said that you were beat be by the military police and anybody else who was able to enter the faculty building where the MUP was located. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you now of your statement presented by the Prosecutor of the 3rd of May, 1997. In English it is on page 3, third paragraph. I'm saying that for Their Honours' benefit. And I'll read out what you said, which is this: "The HVO soldiers took our ID cards and all other particulars and took us to the basement. We came across a man there who we were afraid of. After we arrived, other male Muslims were brought to the cellar too. We were not given any food in the following days. We had to sing. And I and the other Muslim men were beaten up badly during the next two nights. They ordered us to lie down on the floor, and therefore we couldn't see the soldiers."

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to read out something else to you now. There was a correction made to your statement, and the date of that is the 11th of December, 2006, when you arrived in The Hague, and under point 7 you say that: "At the MUP station in Mostar I was beaten up by members of the military police with batons. The people who beat him were wearing HVO military police uniforms." [As interpreted]

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of batons or truncheons are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: "Flagpole," it says.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the difference? So far in the statement it says that you were beaten by the military police and anybody else that managed to enter the premises. Then you said that you couldn't see who beat you because you were lying face down on the floor. And then we have a third statement where you say that it was just the military policemen who beat you. Now, I'm interested in which of these three statements is the right one. Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're all, in fact, correct, because everybody beat me. And people beat me many times. I was beaten many times. Now, in most cases I was not able to see who was doing the beating because we had to assume positions whereby we couldn't see who was beating us, but this time when I was beaten with that flagpole I wasn't lucky enough to throw myself down on the floor straight away, but I was turned towards the door and I was the upper-most on the floor when the policeman came in and hit me. So I received the worst blows. And I saw that particular very hard beating, the very hard blow, and I described that and it was a policeman. So on that one occasion I saw who beat me, and that was the most serious beating and strongest blow and most painful blow that I received. But I was beaten many times, as I say, and many times I wasn't able to see who was doing the beating because we were ordered to lie face down on the floor and not allowed to look. And I did that as soon as possible so that I would be the first to lie down and the other people on top of me, which would protect me from being beaten. But on that particular occasion I wasn't able to throw myself down on the floor quickly enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying you saw who beat you on this one occasion.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when I said that the soldiers had taken our documents away from us, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes I read that from your statement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably said that, but when I refer to soldiers, I usually refer to everybody in uniform as soldiers. So perhaps I didn't remember that actually they were military policemen. I just said off the top of my head "soldiers" because they were in uniform. But everybody who is military engaged, the police or whoever, wearing a uniform I consider to be soldiers. That's the general term I use to refer to all these people. That might have been a mistake on my part.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that on the basis of your statement you're not very well-versed with HVO units, and you don't know who belonged to which unit and what kind of units there were? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how should I explain this to you? Very often I didn't dare look.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant, Witness. Not any specific -- this specific case. But generally speaking, how much do you know about HVO structure? How far are you able to distinguish between their patches, insignia, clothes, uniforms, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much. I didn't dare look at them too much. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do have a few questions for this witness. First of all, I should like to say and I think that this area was broached by my colleague and Judge Trechsel, that is say that Mr. Poryvaev said yesterday that this person was a member of the local defence forces, and in the summary pursuant to 65 ter it says he was a member of the Territorial Defence. So for the record, I wanted to say that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'd like to ask the witness the following: In the past few days we heard that you were in Ljubuski, Mostar, and Heliodrom, in the detention centres there, right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gabela, Capljina, in many locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said you were in Gabela for the first time today. How much time did you spend in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that proceedings have been filed against you and that that's why you were detained?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that. All I do know is that those people together with me went into hiding and that it was our luck that we remembered to make a list of those people because we were being hidden. We were being concealed. Other -- we know that the authorities, BH authorities, were looking for us and the Red Cross was looking for us, and luckily we made these lists and they found us in Gabela on the 31st of December, the Red Cross did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Would you listen to what I'm asking you is it true that court proceedings were taken against you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to show this witness a number of documents. We don't have much time but I think it will be quicker if we provided hard copies to the witness for him to look at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: First document is 6D 00216, and you'll find that on the top of the document it's an order of the 28th of December, 1993. Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 4 it says Ismet Mumin Poljarevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Konjevic Polje"].

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It says with criminal proceedings against prisoners of war that they refer to certain individuals from Gabela. Among those people is your own name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to us when it was that you left Heliodrom exactly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what direction?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I mean when you were finally released from Heliodrom, when you went to Jablanica. So how long were you in Heliodrom for?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st of May, until the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: March, until the 1st of March, Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 7 -- page 7, line 1 it should say Poljarevic and not Konjevic Polje. I'm saying this for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said you left Heliodrom on the 1st of March, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that point in time they pressed charges against you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown another document that was introduced through Witness 181 who was on the list of Prosecution witnesses, P 07985. It's the second document in this series. 7985 is the number, P 07985. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the military prosecutor's office of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. And it also says that criminal reports were filed for crimes committed by certain individuals, and it says pursuant to article so-and-so. Would you now take a look at page 3 and number 90 there. Number 90 on the list on page 3. Ismet Mumin Poljarevic. That's you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page? Page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Page 3, number 90.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have number 90 on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Then it's page 2. Look at the numbers. You'll find your way easier that way.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your name?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that the military prosecutor's office, regardless of the charges against you, allowed the exchange; right? Now, let's have a look at the last page of the document. We have a stamp there. It's not very clear but there's a stamp nonetheless, and a signature. Can you read the word above the signature? What does that say? What does that word say in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Jablanica, the printed word?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, page 3, next to the stamp and signature. What does it say in handwriting there? Does it say "pregledao," reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says reviewed, and then there's a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked this question, Mr. President, when Witness 181 testified, and the -- it's on the transcript number. If counsel can repeat the number. In English it says that it was sent to, delivered to, but in B/C/S "pregledao" means reviewed. And the witness has just affirmed that that is what it says, reviewed by. And the page of the transcript was 10315.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not following. What do you mean reviewed not reviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that the word there is "pregledao" meaning reviewed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The rest of my explanations were given for Their Honours' benefit. May we now go back to document 7183. You've already seen that document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7183 you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a list of persons who are to be isolated.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You recognise some of the names on this document. I'm just making that observation. You've said that you recognise some of the names on this list.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I said I recognise them then I did. You tell me the people and I'll tell it you whether I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is 7183, the number of the document. 7183 for the record. Since the Prosecutor didn't provide us with an explanation, look at the first column where it says RB. You see that RB?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, begin with the first one 375, 189, 317, the RB column and the first numbers?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what do you what happened me to tell me you about them. I don't know these people here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know what these numbers denote, what they mean?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I don't know what they mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Then let's take a look at P 7131, the next document please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: 7131. P 7131. It is dated the 12th of December, 1993. And on this document, if you take a look at it and if we have time, you'll find the same names that are on the other document, 7183, dated the 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who all these people are. Are they all the same or what? I don't know what all these names are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at number 2 on the list, Mustafa Copelj?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and what do you want with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now look at the earlier document that you took a look at, 7183. Page 2, number 2. We find this same name, Mustafa Copelj.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to have that page. What number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's number 2. It says Mustafa Copelj. Alija is his father's name. This document, P 7813, was compiled with an A, B, C order, with the names in A, B, C order. But other documents were used, of the 12th of December, for example, that document was used to compile this A, B, C list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With your permission, and it's short. Witness, on the list 7183, which is alphabetical, do you find your own name? It's rather easy so the list is in alphabetical order. So you probably have to go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance to the witness. The witness didn't find himself on that list but he recognised Poljarevic Zijo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Son of Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have number 135 on this list. Your Honour, I just wanted to say that 7183 is in alphabetical order but the data was used from 7131. And the people are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted it on the record that this -- these are lists where the witness himself does not figure. That was just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question. You said that after Heliodrom you went to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 1st of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When my learned friend asked you that, you said that some people chose to go to third countries.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You chose to go to Jablanica, and you were allowed to do as you wished?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that all the counsel have finished. Is there any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: No thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, this concludes your testimony. I thank you for coming and by contributing to -- with your answers to our efforts to establish the truth. I wish you a safe trip to your country, and I will ask now the usher to escort you out of the courtroom and to bring in the last witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have tried my best to be as truthful, as precise as I could, and I would never wish to say anything wrong or to do any harm to anyone. Thank you again. I did my very best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it's Mr. Kruger and Mr. Mundis who I welcome now. As Mr. Scott just said, the last witness will take two hours all in all, which means that you are not -- two and a half hours all in all, which means you are not going to finish today. You will, therefore, continue tomorrow. And you must do your best to focus on the essential points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Thank you, Your Honour, for that. If I may just mention one aspect. Mr. Scott had previously indicated that he was under the impression that the time on the 65 ter indication was four hours. I had actually given him the wrong estimate. We had thought it would take four hours, but it is indeed a lower estimate that we had from there. But, Your Honour, thank you. The two and a half hours will be sufficient, and I suspect we may even come away in a shorter period, and I have taken on board Your Honour's comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Welcome, Witness. I want to check first of all that you hear the proceedings in the language you understand and that you hear us well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were called by the Prosecution as a witness. Before you give the solemn declaration, give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sejfo Kajmovic, 22nd November, 1951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm working in the administration of the madjlis Islamic community as a secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified as a witness, appeared as a witness before a national or international court concerning events that took place in your country between 1991 and 1995, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down. Witness, just a few explanations. You will now be answering questions first by the Prosecution with whom you met yesterday and the day before yesterday, maybe, during proofing. The Prosecution may also show you some documents to elicit your observations. The overall time of your testimony is scheduled to be two and a half hours, but it may take less than that. Defence counsel are sitting on your left. They will be questioning you as well, and perhaps even the accused who are also on your left, further behind. And the Judges who are in front of you will also ask you for any clarifications that may be required from you following up the questions asked, and we may ask our own questions. If you have any problem, please let us know. And try to be precise in your answers, because your answers and the documents introduced through your testimony will matter to us when we deliberate, and we have to judge on the whole of the evidence, including the evidence presented by the Defence. In due course we will take a break of 20 minutes and continue until 7.00 p.m. We will continue thereafter tomorrow at 2.15 and work until 7.00 p.m. tomorrow. This is how these proceedings work. And I will now give the floor to the Prosecution who will proceed with direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the break, will we be taking that at approximately a quarter to 6.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you wish. We can take the break at a quarter to a quarter to 6.00, at your convenience. It's not a problem for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Sir, is it correct that until July 1993 you were living in Domanovici in the municipality of Capljina?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And more specifically, in Recice, where you were the imam?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you are and at that stage you also were married and you had three daughters?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At that stage, your daughter's ages were 17, 14, and 8 respectively?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: A little less.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The witness is barely audible. He's too far from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The eldest was in the second year of secondary school, the younger one was in primary school, 6th grade, and the very youngest had not started school yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since when had you been -- or from since when had you been the imam in Recice?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: From summer 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Had you at that stage ever been a member of any military organisation or in any army?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No, apart from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just very briefly for the background of -- or for the information of the Judges. Until April 1993, is it correct that you were also a member of the meshihat for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You explained it to me extensively yesterday. If I could sum it up, if you could tell me if this is perhaps accurate, just for the information of the Court, that the meshihat of Bosnia was an elected governing body for religious matters of the Islamic community in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And just to perhaps complete this very brief description, would that be the second level of the overall organisation of the Islamic community which existed at that stage in all the territories comprising the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the meshihat, the executive body of the Islamic community at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you perhaps move just a little bit closer to the microphone so that we're sure that your voice is being picked up. Thank you very much. The -- this organisational structure which you have just described, did that collapse in 1993 or cease to exist in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. With the break-up of the federal state, the SFRY, all the authorities at the level of the common state also dissolved and transformed later into different authorities. Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, during the -- during 1992, when the conflict with the Serbs was ongoing in the area where you lived, is it correct that you left Domanovici for a short period?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Not then. Forty days after the beginning of the conflict I weren't briefly to Brac where my family was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And upon your return, could you tell the Court briefly what the state of your mosque and your house in Recice were?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: They were both in relatively good condition. They were not devastated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you notice any other destruction in your area on your return?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A lot of the houses were already burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And which houses were these?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Mainly Serb houses. They had already been burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, after your return were you joined at some stage by other members of your family who came to live with you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: They were refugees from the area where they had come from, Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Members of my extended family if I can put it that way. My immediate family was at the isle of Brac after the outbreak of the conflict. My parents came, my brother with his child, my in-laws, and some other close relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were any members of this extended family of yours who became members of the military during that time or during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No, none of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if we can turn briefly to a different topic. During 1993, is it correct that you were involved with -- with the humanitarian organisation Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In what capacity were you involved?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of that body and I was in charge of supplies, procurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What -- very briefly, what was the main goal of Merhamet during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The main goal was to procure food, mainly flour for the refugees, and not only refugees but also the local population who had by that time been impoverished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The focus of Merhamet, was it a specific ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's mainly the Bosniak population, because the Croats were supplied by Caritas, and we, both of us, got most of the supplies from UNHCR. We also took care of a couple of Serb families that had not moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from supplying food did -- was any form of medical services supplied or supported by Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a clinic in Capljina where professional doctors and nurses worked, and we had a pharmacy attached with quite a good choice of medication, at least under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The clinic and the pharmacy, did they only provide services to Bosniaks or also to others?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: To everybody, everybody who addressed themselves to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if we can move to a further topic. In 1993, the Court has heard of tensions rising between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosniaks, also in your area. Could you tell us in this regard about what you know about what occurred at the Capljina high school?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: In that high school in Capljina, there was a spontaneous rebellion of Bosniak students, because the emblems and iconography of Herceg-Bosna were displayed. And because the Croat language was introduced in what I would call an aggressive way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And was this in -- were these introduced as the only symbols or were they -- and language, or were they introduced parallel to existing symbols and language in use in the school?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Everything else was eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the -- what effect, if any, did the October 1992 and January 1993 conflicts in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf have on you and other Bosniaks living in your area?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that had repercussions on our area where I lived, Capljina, because tensions grew and there was more mistrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In the first half of 1993 what media were you able to receive in your area, television and then written media?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I think we could watch Television Sarajevo and two Croatian channels, I believe, the first and the second programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Before turning to the written media, by July 1993, were all these channels still available, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: These two channels were still available. I'm not sure about the BH channel, because the repeater was destroyed then. I don't know how long we were able to watch them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You say these two channels. Are you referring to the two Croatian channels?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian channels. We had better reception from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what about the written media, newspapers and magazines, topical magazines? What was available to you and your community or area in the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Newspapers and magazines from Croatia, some local press, and the others were physically unable to be delivered because of the situation on the roads towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was this different -- a different situation than what had existed previously?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The tensions had an effect, and the situation certainly deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry. What I mean -- I wasn't clear. My apology. Regarding media, the availability of media that you have just described, was there prior to this period in 1993, was there a wider variety available at any stage?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that we had many more before. The delivery of newspapers and magazines was already very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'd like to turn to the presence of the HVO in the area where you lived during 1993. Now, in Domanovici after the -- the Serb occupation had been terminated, did the HVO establish a presence in Domanovici?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And where did they establish this?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: At the entrance to Domanovici. In fact, there was a mental hospital there, and that was used -- that building was used as a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The -- if you say the entrance to Domanovici, would -- from which direction would that have been the entrance?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Looking from Capljina on the left-hand side as you enter Domanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know which HVO unit was at this location?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were some outfits, some units of that Prince Domagoj unit from Capljina, because it was their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, the Prince Domagoj unit, is that to your knowledge the same as the Knez Domagoj unit?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm wrong about the name, but I know exactly which unit that was stationed in the Grabovina barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of this unit was?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew it was Colonel Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, apart from -- from the barracks which was established in the psychiatric -- old psychiatric hospital, was there at any stage or did any other -- or was any other location used by the HVO in Domanovici?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a while they used the building of the primary school, but that was later, just before the conflict, the expulsions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So by the end of June 1993, were both of these locations which you have mentioned occupied by or used by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the second location you've mentioned in the primary school, did the presence of the HVO at that location cause any problems in any way or disturbance for the local inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think their presence caused great fear and concern, because that's the way they acted, in an intimidating way, and their very appearance was intimidating. They were wearing black uniforms, and they looked frightening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you describe any specific actions which intimidated or which you felt were intimidating?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until late at night there would be Ustasha songs sung and broadcast over the PA system, and that was certainly a great disturbance to all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you say across or over the PA system, was this an internal PA system or an external PA system?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: It must have been external as well, because we could hear it very well outside of that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you hear this from your own house?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You could hear it even further away, a lot further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How far is your house away from -- from this location where the primary school was?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: My school? If you mean my mekteb, it was close to the mosque and close to my house. So it was about a kilometre away. Next to the road towards Stolac, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can move to April, 1993, specifically, Witness, what do you know about the arrest of Bosniak males from the period of April onwards? What did you experience yourself or see?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I know when the arrests started and when people, Bosniak intellectuals were selectively incarcerated. Many of my friends were incarcerated at that time. I was kept abreast of the situation. I knew what it was about. It all instilled fear in us. Each one of us expected to be arrested, and there was general uncertainty. So that was what the situation was like. You could have -- great psychological pressure was being exerted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you at any stage visit or try to visit any of the people who were incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did my best, and I managed to visit them for the Bajram holiday. Beginning of June 1993, I visited them. I went to see them in the barracks in Grabovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How was -- before doing that did you go alone or were you accompanied by others?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Three of my friends went along with me from my parish or dzemat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How were you clothed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I had black clothing. We call it dzubba. It was the official type of clothing, and I had the official type of cap on my head with the white - what shall I say? - white band around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How had this visit been arranged?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How had the visit been arranged?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we managed to collect some food since it was Bajram. There were a lot of cakes, sweets, cigars, juices. We organised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know how permission was obtained or how this was coordinated with the authorities at the Grabovina barracks?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was authorised by the colonel, the commander, Obradovic. Otherwise, we wouldn't have been able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What did you find? How did this visit go when you got there?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, from my perspective it was a risk. It was risky business. We weren't quite sure what would happen. We thought we would be sent back. And there was increased tension at the time because of the conflicts in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf. So that was an additional aggravating situation. But we succeeded, and we managed to pay them a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the officials involved in the detention?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In front of the building where these intellectuals had been detained Bosko Previsic, who I think was the commander of - what should I call it? - a prison, came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Bosko Previsic, did you know Bosko Previsic at that stage or who he was?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I didn't have any contact with him. He was a waiter by profession, so quite possibly might have seen him around but, no, we didn't have any communication. I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you come across him again later that year?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: In Gabela camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that. Now, Witness, on that day, early in June when you visited the intellectuals at Grabovina barracks, what was -- what was the reaction or what did Boko Previsic do on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: He was there when we arrived. There wasn't any physical abuse. Well, he was a little insulting and delivered a lecture to us, but he gave us 10 minutes to visit. We couldn't do much in 10 minutes, but there were detainees up on the floor above and down below, so we went upstairs, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can move from there to the 30th of June of 1993. And on that day, can you tell the Court, when you were coming from Split with a Merhamet convoy, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were coming back from Split with the Merhamet convoy, and at the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, in Doljani, we were arrested. The truck was seized and -- the trucks were seized and the drivers were arrested, and our car was confiscated and we were taken to Dretelj. The four of us who were in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, who were the four of you who were in the car?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: There was myself, then the main Capljina imam, Hasan Palic, the president of Merhamet, Hadji Alija Suta, and Zlatar Buzaljko, who went to procure some medicines for the chemist of the -- Merhamet, of which he was the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, how many trucks were in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I think five trucks. Fifty tonnes of goods we were carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What were the goods on the trucks?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly flour, some medicines. I don't know that there was anything else, but mostly flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was the convoy in possession of documentation authorising the transport of these goods?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our documents were in order when we left Capljina and when the goods were loaded up and, upon our return, all the documents were in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say the documents were in order when you left Capljina, by whom had these documents been issued, or by what authority?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the authority responsible for that kind of thing. Mr. Dzevanica. He signed it, and he would issue permits of that kind or authorisation. Or some of his colleagues. But the authority in charge of travel and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And was there any letterhead on -- used for this documentation?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the usual type of letterhead. I didn't look at the papers because the president of the Merhamet went there. So it was the standard type of Herceg-Bosna letterhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So Mr. Zevanica or Dzevanica, was he an official of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you -- had you seen when the goods were loaded on this -- on the trucks for this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the warehouse. The procedure was the same. No separate procedure, just like the type of procedure applied when any goods are being loaded up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, were there any weapons or ammunition being transported on these trucks?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were taken to Dretelj. Do you know what happened to the trucks, the freight on the trucks and on your car? Were any of these everybody returned to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, upon arrival in Dretelj, at what time did you arrive in Dretelj approximately on the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Towards evening. If we take it that it was a summer's day, after 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And on arrival at Dretelj was it only your group that arrived there or were there other people also arriving or present?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I really didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who took you to Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The police, the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And from which organisation?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, at Dretelj how long did you personally stay there?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Until about midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In that period that you stayed there, what did you see or what was -- what did you experience?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Since we were there at the entrance itself right up against the gates, there wasn't much I could see, but we were verbally abused by drunken or tipsy soldiers, but not any physical abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: These drunken or tipsy soldiers, from which army were they?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: HVO. It was the HVO barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, is it correct that you and imam Hasan Palic were then released and taken home by the HVO to your respective homes?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometime after midnight they took me away in a police car to Domanovici, and then he was taken to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, from that period on the Court has heard that Bosniak males were being arrested. Did you see or witness or experience any of this in your area or know of it?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Already from that time the arrests became more intensive, the arrests of Bosniaks, that is. It was done on a more massive scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And how did that affect you personally? What was your reaction to this arrest taking place?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was frightened, of course, for myself, but even more so for my family and for the parishioners. And you never knew when they would come and take away someone close to you without any explanation, without any intimation. They would just come and take them off to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if I can now turn or jump to the 13th of July, and could you tell the Court what you experienced on the morning of the 13th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July in the morning very early on we were woken up by some shooting. My family and I woke up. We got up. We saw that something was going on. We were frightened, of course, because we didn't know what it was all about. But quite obviously there was some armed conflict going on because you could see the traces of it already. There was fighting at Satorova Glavica, and some of the bushes and trees were on fire up there, so quite obviously there was a conflict. We didn't know what it was all about, but we realised soon enough and knew that we had to do something to leave that place, to evacuate ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, at this stage I would like to go through the witness's evidence with the assistance of a map which would help to orientate the Court, but as the map may be up on the screen and the witness may be marking it in a period of about 15 minutes, this is perhaps the best time to -- to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to take a break now, then. It's almost 5.35, so we reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before having a look at a map, you mentioned that there was some kind of armed conflict going on or some fighting going on. Did you know at that stage or do you have any idea between whom this fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I didn't know the persons, but I knew there was a conflict between Bosniaks. I don't know in which form they were organised, but it was a conflict between Bosniaks and the HVO. There could be no other conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if I could request the usher to put Exhibit 09789 on the e-court. Sir, I'm going to show you a map now. It's a very rough map of Capljina. It's the one I showed you yesterday as well. Thank you. And if we could zoom in on the -- that's right. Thank you. Now, Witness, we have zoomed in on the map. Do you recognise that as a part that we had a look at yesterday, part of the larger map?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know that area well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the -- I'm going to ask you to mark a few places in the course of your testimony as we progress through it, and I'm going to ask you to mark those places or locations on the screen. The very first thing I want you to do is if you could mark with an X the approximate location of your house and mosque.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Around here. A kilometre away from the intersection towards Radovanovici on the way to Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That intersection that you refer to, is that also where the HVO barracks was, in the psychiatric hospital or the old psychiatric hospital?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The barracks is at the entirely different end of Domanovici. You had to pass Domanovici and go on and then the barracks remains behind you towards the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, could you mark the entrance which you refer to where -- where that barracks was. And if you could mark it with a circle?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: So this is the exit from Domanovici towards Capljina. It's around here, from the main road towards Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the crossroads, is that a located at the star which appears just to the right of that circle you've just made?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: This little star, yes. That's the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before moving on, in your religious community did you know Hasan Hasic?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him well, for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you mark --

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: From our very arrival there, 18 and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you mark with a number 1 the approximate location of his house?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: From the intersection at Domanovici, if you go -- if you follow the road towards Mostar, after about 200 metres [as interpreted] there is a village road leading to a Mahala called Glavica, and his house is the second one from the road on the left. That's Hasan's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you make a number 1 at that cross so that we can distinguish that.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that you could see fighting in the area of Satorova Glavica. Could you mark with the number 2 the approximate location of Satorova Glavica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] It's wrong in the record. It's not 200 kilometres. It's 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. It's metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, we'll return to this map in a few moments. You mentioned earlier, just before the break, that you knew you had to do something to leave that place, to evacuate yourselves. So what did you and your family do when you heard the fighting that morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Kruger, but you yourself have interrupted yourself. The witness was about to show us where - what was the name? - Satorova Glavica was and you were interrupted. Maybe you want to go back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that a number 2 is marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, Witness, I see that you have marked the number 2 on your screen. Is that the location of Satorova Glavica?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's Satorova Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, where did you and your family go when you heard the fighting on that morning?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: To the opposite side from the direction where the shooting was coming from, across the road and to the south, south-east. Towards -- yes, you could say south-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And was -- was this a forest that you went to essentially?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, could you mark on this map with a line -- sorry. Could you mark with a line the approximate location of the forest where you went.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the woods. From the road to this side where we went it's approximately here. It takes up part of Oplicici village and part of the river, the riverlet. It's not really a traditional forest. There are many orchard, vineyards, peach orchards, et cetera, but there's a lot of woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you mark that line, somewhere on the line, just with a number 3 so that we can distinguish it.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, is it correct that close to your house there was a hill called Podkosa or Potkosa? Could --

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you mark that -- could you mark that as well. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Here. Approximately towards the turn towards Lokva, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And that is a number 4 that you've put there for us.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in -- in this area where you stayed this -- this -- if we could describe it as a forest, how long did you stay in this area?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there -- not in the woods. We were in the woods towards -- during the day, but we slept in the Mahala. We spent two nights in Oplicici, in the neighbouring village. So from the 13th to the 17th, on the day when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I don't know whether it was interpreted, but I heard you mention the name Cuckovina. Did I hear incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cuckovina is a hamlet in my parish, in my dzemat in Oplicici village, and it's to the south-east of my house and my mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you mark the area of Cuckovina with a number 6, please.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could mark one more location on this, and that is if you could mark the approximate location of the mosque in Aladinici, while we're busy with the map. And mark that with a 5, please. We haven't used 5.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could capture -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could make your initial at the bottom of the map in the right-hand corner. If you could put SK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, for the record, the registrar tells me it's P 09276. In fact, there are two numbers for this same map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. The case manager has just informed me on that, Your Honour. I think I was working on the other one. Is the -- is the previous one already admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to give it an IC number, and that's going to deal with the problem. Please, an IC number registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number IC 177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could keep the map up on the screen for -- it will help in understanding the following testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, now, the fighting that you heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petkovic? THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to help the witness make a correction. Under number 5 it's not the road to Aladinici. You got it wrong. The road to Aladinici goes to the right, and we are talking about the mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. It's on the road towards Stolac. You're right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, did you have any comment to make or -- as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Aladinici are on the road towards Stolac. So the suggestion is absolutely correct and justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you wish to make any correction, then, to the diagrams that you have indicated, or is that not necessary?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's very important. Yes, it's very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What correction did you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: It's easy to mark it, Aladinici, the location on the road towards Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I see. So that number 5 that you have indicated, did you wish to -- to relocate that, that mark?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's around three kilometres from the intersection towards Lokva. That's where Aladinici is. The mosque is on the left of the road, right on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you then scratch out the -- or eliminate the first number 5 that you've made.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The legal officer tells me that we should have given it another number with this modification. So for this revised map, what is going to be the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number IC 178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Petkovic for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, Witness, in the period -- sorry. To return to my old question, the fighting that you heard on the morning of the 13th of July, 1993, did that continue or did that stop or die down at some stage?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at some point. In fact, I probably didn't even hear the real shooting, but later it quieted down and turned into sporadic fire, three and four hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you see from where you were any troops in the area or the movement of any troops, soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Which soldiers or what soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I was able to see the movement of troops on that road towards Stolac, towards Lokva. That part of the road was visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what troops could you see on that road, if you could identify them?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was HVO troops. At least that's what I thought then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in your mind on that day and then in the following few days that you were in that area, did you have any idea which army controlled the area surrounding where you were?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was obvious that the HVO took control of that entire area and was holding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if we can move to the question of mosques in the area. Could you from that area see any part of your mosque?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: From my position I could not see all of my mosque. I could maybe see the -- the upper half of the minaret. I would have had to come closer, and that was quite risky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did you observe anything with regard to your mosque in the period that you were in this forest?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I only saw the smoke when it was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I really didn't keep a diary. I could get the date wrong easily, but all that I'm talking about happened between the 13th and the 17th, the four days that I was there. It could have been the next day. So the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Subsequent to seeing smoke at your mosque, did you have the occasion during that period, those four days, to actually see your mosque and your house?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next day I was in a better position to see it, because already the next day it was possible to see better. The HVO was concentrated along that line. And my father went there that same evening, and when he came back he what had happened. In fact, we didn't even know that he had left us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what did your father tell you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that the mosque had been set on fire, that our house had burnt down. We used to have one cow. We didn't have time to untie it, and anyway, we thought it was not going to last. So unfortunately the house -- the cow burned too. It was in a makeshift shed behind the house. It was actually a garage that we had turned into a shed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After your father had told you this, did you with your own eyes have an occasion or chance to see your house and mosque?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The ashes, the ruins, that everything was burned down as he had said. Of course I didn't go there, but I came close enough to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From the forest could you see any other mosques in the area or in the region?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw two mosques in Lokva and in Aladinici. I could see them the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did you observe anything with regard to these two mosques?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them burn. They were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In relation to your own mosque in Recice, could you give the Court an indication whether it was the same day or later?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the next day, in the evening. That's when I saw flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you saw these flames were both of these mosques alight at the same time or at different times?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: They burned at the same time. I saw them burning. I don't know when they were set on fire, but they were burning simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And at the time when they were burning, around that time was there still fighting in the area of those mosques that you observed or heard?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no more fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At that stage, according to your observations, who was in control of the areas where these mosques were situated?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: HVO, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in this area where you were -- where you and your family had taken refuge, were other people also hiding in this area?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who were these people who were also hiding there?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mainly from the settlements closer to the road from Domanovici and such, people who were in the first line of fire, and that's why they went into hiding probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I have a question. You just said that there were three mosques that burned, yours, the one in Lokva, and the one in Aladinici. You said that you went to see your mosque, and you said there were just ashes left. What I want know is, when you saw with your own eyes your mosque, were you able to determine how it was set on fire? Was it a shell that fell on it? Was there explosive set and then it was blown up? Was it accidentally set on fire? Was it torched with an incendiary device or a flammable substance? Were you able to determine how it burned?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on what was going on at the time and my own conclusions, I decided that it was set on fire deliberately because there were no shells. I think it was simply torched. It was not blown up, although such things happened later during the war, but it was simply set on fire deliberately, arsoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was set on fire, but how? Do you have anything that could help us understand how the fire caught on, or you cannot help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the other people who were also in this forest, what was the -- what were they hiding from or why were they hiding, for the record.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, primarily out of fear. They feared retaliation. They feared mistreatment. They feared they might be killed. I don't know what was going through each one of their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were these people all Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can move to the 17th of July. Before doing that, may I just ask you one more question on this. Did you see anything else apart from mosques burning or being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Many Bosniak houses were aflame in Lokva, Aladinici, Satorova Glava. You could even see part of Bivolje Brdo. Houses were on fire there, too. So this was done systematically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, on the 17th of July, 1993, at that stage you were in the hamlet of Cuckovina with your family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The first and last night we spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And tell the Court how it came that you left that location on that day.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning of that day, the 17th of July, a young man from the neighbourhood came by and said -- and said to the people who I was staying with, me, my family were guests there, that at 5.00 they should be ready, that trucks would come to evacuate them from Cuckovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In young man from the neighbourhood, was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did this soldier tell you where you would be going to or what would happen to you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said for our own safety mostly that we would be taken elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At 5.00 that day did trucks then arrive or a truck?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several trucks arrived, and they took some from the village. So the people went in their own trucks, some of them. We sat on the hub of the trucks and travelled that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you have a choice in this matter? Could you have remained where you were?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not really. We didn't have a choice, just to escape. But that wasn't a choice, really, a viable one, because the risk was very great.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Where did the trucks go when you were on them?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: We went via Domanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. And to where?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: At the time there was a well-known catering establishment called Han. It was done in the oriental fashion. So that's where we were unloaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. That's a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor. Just a short question. You were speaking of trucks. Were they military trucks and, if so, who did they belong to? Did they have any insignia, any markings on those trucks that you were transporting the people, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they were civilian trucks, and the drivers were civilians too. They weren't military trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the trucks were requisitioned by the HVO or what? Or were they civilians that wanted to help the population to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that they didn't want to go voluntarily. I think the HVO took them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, Witness, you were busy telling us about the catering establishment Han. Could you continue from there? Where is Han?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Han is located in Pocitelj. It's an old town, and it's in the oriental style, all the buildings. There's a mosque. There was the Madrasa or religious school, the hamam during Turkish times. There's a large artists' colony too. It was functioning during the war. So it was an oriental town. Everything is in the oriental style, all the facilities and buildings and features.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you arrived there on that night, were all of these buildings still intact?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't notice anything amiss, anything that had been set fire to or devastated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Until when did you remain in Pocitelj?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Until about 9.00. Roughly 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what happened at 9.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: They rounded up the men, loaded them up, and took them away. They were to separate the men from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO. I mean the HVO, the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say "HVO, the police," would this be military police or not?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, before looking at what happened to you further, just briefly, what happened to your family after this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Mr. Kruger. There was a question that you don't seem to be asking, so I'll ask it. You've just said that they were separated, that the military HVO police separated them, the people. Now, how could you distinguish between HVO soldiers and HVO military policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was able to do that quite clearly. The military police wore white belts and had white equipment. That is to say belts, pistols cases, batons or truncheons, and I think they're easily distinguishable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There we have some precise information. Mr. Kruger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, Witness, could you briefly tell the Court what happened to your family after you had been taken away from Pocitelj.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: My family, just like many other families who went with me, and even some after and before, found some accommodation in Pocitelj. There were some weekend cottages and houses where they put up, and they stayed there. Perhaps even for as long as 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And at the end of that period what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I know that after that they were taken by the HVO in trucks crossing Western Herzegovina to Jablanica, I think. But they went for a sort of exchange which never took place. I don't know for what reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: On that evening where were you taken when you were loaded on the trucks?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: They drove us directly to Gabela camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive at Gabela camp approximately?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was about 11.00, thereabouts. About 11.00. That is 2300 hours I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In the evening. So on your arrival at 11.00 in the evening, what -- what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: We were loaded out of the trucks. We were all in one truck. We were lined up at the gate. We stood there for about an hour. We were verbally abused, interrogated, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if you say "we," who are you referring to? "We were all in one truck and lined up at the gate."

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I mean myself and the people who were with me in my group, some 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did any other people or were any other people arriving at Gabela on that evening?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I assume so, but I'm not sure. They were brought in later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The people in your group, were they all Bosniak males?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all Bosniak, and they were all from Cuckovina, the same settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What about your brother? Was he with you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my brother was with me, too. He was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
