utterances.text: If you say that on arrival you were verbally abused, interrogated, that kind of thing, who was verbally abusing you and interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I just know that his name was Marko, a well-built man, very rough. Athletically built, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was he the only person on your arrival at Gabela, that is, to receive you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: He mistreated us and questioned us, and, by the gate, there was the boss of Bosko Previsic. His name was Nikola Andrun. He was sitting there but didn't say anything or do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Marko and Nikola Andrun, were they dressed in any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What typed ever uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Marko was wearing some sort of - what shall I call it? - T-shirt, like Rambo, with the braces and the trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Both of these persons during your stay in Gabela, did both of these persons remain in Gabela or were they only there at that night, on that night?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were there for a longer period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So after your reception as you've described, where were you put in the camp, in -- in the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: We were put in hanger number 3, the third in line. And we were to the right of the door. I suppose there was still some room there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In hangar number 3 when you went into that hangar on that night, what was your impression or your experience? Please describe that for the Court.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all there, wasn't much room. We couldn't lie down. We couldn't even sit comfortably. We were up against each other. And that's how dawn came. I couldn't see anything, but I could imagine what was going on. I heard some sounds and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When dawn came, could you gain an impression of how many people were in that hangar?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that it was already full there was several hundred people there. Of course I couldn't count them, but the hangar was certainly full.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, this hanger, did it have windows and doors which were open?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It had two doors, wide doors, and windows which were high up, right under the roof, and they were closed. So was the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you describe the quality of the air as you experienced it in that hangar?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The air. Well, there wasn't any air any more. We were like fish out of water. We couldn't breathe. It was humid and hot. People had relieved themselves, defecated, urinated. People sweated. Some had been beaten up and had been injured. It was just terrible, deplorable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How was food provided upon your arrival and in the first period you remained in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I was lucky and got a meal the very next day, lunch. The people who were arrested before me had had nothing to eat, but we were all given that first meal, lunch. And what I got, well, it was distributed from a large receptacle into the typical military army rations, army dishes. There weren't enough of these dishes to go around, so you'd have to eat up quickly so that the next person could get your plate. And it was a very modest lunch, just two or three spoons of some liquid and a piece of cabbage and a small piece of bread, because a loaf of bread would be divided into 15, 16, or even 18 pieces, and that was the daily meal for a period of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that was the meal you received on the first day. In comparison to this, how were the meals that you received in the subsequent period?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The other meals were better than the first meal but certainly not enough to quench your hunger. There would be some peas or macaroni from time to time, but the piece of bread was always very small and thin and not enough, of course. Whatever there was, there was not enough of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, after the first day when you received one meal, in the subsequent period did you receive more than one meal a day or not?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No. For a whole month just one meal of that type, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was the situation regarding water?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The water situation was even more critical. We hardly ever received any water, to begin with, or just a symbolic amount, seven or eight litres to be divided among 400 inmates. Sometimes it would be better if they didn't bring us any water at all, because it only caused a great deal of trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was the effect of -- of this little amount of water that was received? What was the effect on you and the other detainees in that hangar?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it made us even more thirsty it, because you couldn't really get even a drop of water. So we were more thirsty, if anything. And of course we dehydrated very quickly. We sweated a lot and didn't take any liquid in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know of any people who were with you in that camp who suffered any consequences, long-term consequences, as a result of this lack of water and dehydration?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think I'm one of them. I have difficulties and problems with my kidneys and my intestines. And I know that some -- one of the men there, his kidneys ceased to function. I was a neighbour of mine, Vahid Lizda. So already -- this happened already to him in the camp. He was taken ill and transported to hospital, and I think he had a transplant. Anyway, he's still alive. But, yes, it did have an effect on one's body and one vital organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The personnel at Dretelj detention centre -- sorry. My apologies. At Gabela detention centre, to your mind, were they aware of the effect of the lack of water and food and the effect it was having on the detainees?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. They certainly knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was obvious that the people were suffering. Many of them started losing consciousness, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The commander at the detention centre, Bosko Previsic, according to what you know was he aware of what was going on and of the condition of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully. He was fully aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And on what basis do you say so?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that he was kept abreast of everything. He saw the kind of food that came in, how the people reacted. He was present there very often. He could see it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you ever observe him, in your hangar, address detainees where you were present?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, many times. Almost every morning. He would come by and lecture us, hold forth, with abuses of course. He would hold a monologue. Sometimes he would come in the afternoon and towards evening. He would say things, do something, organise a raid. He would come in almost every day, and we would hear this monologue of his delivered to us, which was very demeaning for us and insulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, upon your arrival in the hangar, you've described the conditions. Could I ask you to describe whether you saw any injuries on any of the people that you encountered in that hangar.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Already in the morning I saw a terrible scene. I saw many people who had been beaten up. It was quite obvious that they had experienced various kinds of torture. I don't know whether while they were being arrested or whether when they were already there, but probably both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And from what did you see or what specific injuries or conditions did you see?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing I noticed, as soon as it was daylight, to my right there were two men sitting down. They were neighbours, actually, from Rotimlja. I know their surnames. I'm not sure of their first names, though. One was a blonde young guy, Behram, and I think the other was Safro. He had blonde hair and was of athletic build. This first one Behram, his eye was closed up and he had bruises all over his body and I even gained the impression that his ribs had been broken. He found it very hard to breathe. This other man, on his chest he had a wound, an injury on his chest. It was an open wound, and it had already become infected. You could see the signs of infection setting in. And somebody later on said that when he was being arrested they burnt him with a piece of paper. Anyway, he had this burn injury on his chest. There were other people, too. Two brothers, Dzonko. I can't remember what their first names were, but I know that their father's name was Halil. They were beaten up too. But I think that this was when they were arrested. It had already happened when they were being arrested. Of course, there were people being beaten up there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody being beaten inside your hangar, hangar number 3?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court about that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a group enter, a group of several men, and among them was a tall guy, a tall policeman wearing the military police uniform, and he had a truncheon, and with them was an athletically built young man with a broad belt with some metal spikes or plaques or whatever around that belt. It was probably a heavy belt. And I think he wore it in order to beat people with it. So when this group entered they asked where Zuhric was, and right next to me there were several people called Zuhric from Oplicici. And there was a father and son Zuhrici from my own village, from Recice. And they came forward and they started beating them in front of us. The policeman was the most brutal. He would use his truncheon to beat these people, the Zuhrici. There was a young man or rather a young boy; Zuhric was his name, too. I can't remember his first name, but Mujo was his father's name, so this was Mujo's son, Zuhric. They took him outside the camp, placed him up against the wall and used the truncheon to beat him. He screamed and moaned until he fell down. The other Zuhrics were beaten up inside. They were beaten with the truncheon on the body and face. They were kicked. One day, perhaps a few days after my arrest, another Zuhric was brought in from -- the one from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may interrupt you for a moment before you proceed on this. The tall policeman where the military police uniform that you refer to, which military police was -- uniform was this?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO. The HVO. Nobody else could have entered anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The other men who were in this group, were they military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the civilian, the athletic type. And later, people around me told me that he was allegedly from Split. A body-building type, as they referred to him, from Split. And he would generally come in to beat up the inmates, the prisoners. I can't remember all the others, but that was the time when anybody was free to enter and beat up the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The -- these persons who came in on that day, do I understand correctly from what you say that they were not attached to Gabela detention centre? They didn't have any official function there as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were the personnel at Gabela aware of the entry of these persons into the facility and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did know, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And why do you say so?

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm quite sure they knew, quite sure. They had to see them. They had to go in through the gate. They -- I'm sure they knew all about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry I interrupted you. You were just about to tell us about another Zuhric that was brought in, one the one from your village.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I was going to say was this: Elvis Zuhric, when they arrested him, they took him to the barracks in Grabovina, and he was beaten up there. So that he was -- they carried him in and brought him in to where we were. And his father, the other Mujo Zuhric, so not the first man that I mentioned but his father Mujo Zuhric, was rounded up and taken off and he never returned. He was killed, in fact. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the instances that you have mentioned of beatings that you have seen, were these the only instances that you saw? Did you also see other instances? Without going into details, just to find out if there were other instances.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were. When the group arrived, the group that would go outside the barracks to do some kind of labour. They would be searched, and as a rule mostly this was done by the commander, Boko. And if he were to find any cigarettes or tins of any kind, then the person would receive a blow to the head with a rifle or rifle butt. I saw a man called Sabanovic, a young guy, well-built, when -- he hit him and he went around with this bruise for a long time. He was hit in the forehead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEJFO KAJMOVIC
utterances.text: And I also saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you at that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it is 7.00. I estimate about another 20 to 25 minutes with the witness for tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. It is 7.00. We're going to adjourn for the day and reconvene for the last day of the year. The hearing starts tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.
